content: 1. Kinslow K (2016) conducted a study on the human health impacts of litter on beaches, focusing on the perceptions of cleanliness on Tasmanian beaches. The findings were published in Ocean & Coastal Management (Volume 126, Pages 22–30). 2. Castelli PM and Sleggs SE (2000) evaluated the effectiveness of using border collies to manage nuisance Canada geese populations. Their research was published in the Wildlife Society Bulletin (Volume 13, Pages 385–392). 3. Conover MR and Chasko GG (1985) investigated the problems caused by nuisance Canada geese in the eastern United States. Their findings appeared in the Wildlife Society Bulletin (Volume 13, Pages 228–233). 4. Currie DC and Adler PH (2008) explored the global diversity of black flies (Diptera: Simuliidae) in freshwater ecosystems. Their work was published in Hydrobiologia (Volume 595, Pages 469–475). 5. The Department of Environmental Health (2017) in Argentina issued sanitary guidelines for the safe use of recreational waters, focusing on enteropathogens and opportunistic microorganisms in aquatic environments. 6. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) (2014) released guidelines for the surveillance of native mosquito species in Europe, accessible as a PDF document. 7. The ECDC also provided an expert fact sheet on phlebotomine sandflies, detailing their role as disease vectors, accessible online. 8. The European Mosquito Control Association (EMCA) (2011) published guidelines for controlling mosquitoes of public health importance in Europe, available as a PDF. 9. Goodwin KD et al. (2017) examined the role of natural sources in bacterial Total Maximum Daily Load (TMDL) assessments, including microbial source tracking on beaches. Their study was published in Environmental Science & Technology (Volume 51, Issue 14, Pages 7775–7784). 10. Haddad V et al. (2018) reported on mass envenomations caused by jellyfish blooms affecting aquatic marathon participants in southern and southeastern Brazil. The cases were documented in Wilderness & Environmental Medicine (Volume 29, Pages 142–145). 11. Health Canada (2012) issued the third edition of its guidelines for Canadian recreational water quality, emphasizing public health protection. 12. Hoellein TJ et al. (2015) studied the abundance and environmental drivers of anthropogenic litter on five Lake Michigan beaches, utilizing citizen science data collection. Their findings were published in the Journal of Great Lakes Research (Volume 41, Pages 78–86). 13. Jordon DW et al. (2019) investigated the exclusion of ring-billed gulls from recreational beaches using canid harassment techniques. Their research was published in The Condor (Volume 121, Issue 1). 14. The Joint Research Centre of the European Commission (JRC/EC) released reports in 2016 and 2020 addressing various environmental issues, available as PDFs. 15. Keep Scotland Beautiful (2018) published the My Beach, Your Beach Phase One Report, summarizing findings from the summer of 2018. 16. Khairunnisa AK et al. (2012) analyzed the composition and abundance of marine debris on selected beaches in Port Dickson, Malaysia. Their study appeared in Aquatic Ecosystem Health & Management (Volume 9, Pages 147–158). 17. Kiessling T et al. (2019) described a project where schoolchildren sampled litter along German rivers, estimating sources and types of riverside litter. The study was published in Environmental Pollution (Volume 245, Pages 545–557). 18. Kuo F-J and Huang H-W (2014) proposed strategies for mitigating marine debris, analyzing its sources and composition in northern Taiwan. Their work was published in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 83, Pages 70–78). 19. Laglbauer BJL et al. (2014) investigated macrodebris and microplastics on Slovenian beaches, publishing their findings in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 89, Pages 356–366). 20. Lopes da Silva M et al. (2015) conducted a spatial-temporal analysis of marine debris on beaches in Niterói, Brazil, focusing on Itaipu and Itacoatiara. Their study appeared in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 92, Pages 233–236). 21. Madkour FF et al. (2019) documented the aggregation of the alien tropical jellyfish Rhopilema nomadica along the Mediterranean coast of Egypt. Their findings were published in the International Marine Science Journal (Volume 1, Issue 2, Pages 1–7). 22. Mansour G et al. (2017) evaluated cleanup endpoint parameters for sandy beaches polluted with heavy fuel oil. Their research was published in Cogent Environmental Science (Volume 3, Article 1391676). 23. Montgomery L et al. (2016) reviewed envenomation and treatment options for European jellyfish species, publishing their findings in Marine Drugs (Volume 14, Issue 7, Article 127). 24. Mouat J et al. (2010) examined the economic aspects of marine litter, with their findings accessible as a PDF. 25. Munari C et al. (2016) analyzed the composition, spatial distribution, and sources of marine litter on Mediterranean shores, focusing on northwestern Adriatic beaches. Their study was published in Waste Management (Volume 49, Pages 483–490). 26. Nelms SE et al. (2017) conducted a 10-year nationwide assessment of marine anthropogenic litter on British beaches using citizen science data. Their findings were published in Science of the Total Environment (Volume 579, Pages 1399–1409). 27. Ocean Conservancy (2019) released a report titled The Beach and Beyond, accessible as a PDF. 28. The OSPAR Commission (2010) provided guidelines for monitoring marine litter on beaches within the OSPAR maritime area. 29. Pitt KA and Purcell JE (2009) edited a book on jellyfish blooms, discussing their causes, consequences, and recent advances, published by Springer. 30. Purcell JE et al. (2007) reviewed anthropogenic causes of jellyfish blooms and their direct consequences for humans, publishing their findings in Marine Ecology Progress Series (Volume 350, Pages 153–174). 31. Quail MT (2019) discussed the health risks associated with sea lice and seabather’s eruption in warm waters, publishing the findings in Nursing (Volume 49, Issue 1, Pages 40–43). 32. Rayon-Viña F et al. (2018) analyzed marine litter in the South Bay of Biscay, linking local differences in beach littering to citizen perception and awareness. Their study appeared in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 131, Pages 727–735). 33. Remigante A et al. (2018) reviewed the impact of scyphozoan venoms on human health and current first aid options for stings, publishing their findings in Toxins (Volume 10, Article 133). 34. Scanlan CM et al. (2007) monitored opportunistic macroalgal blooms for the Water Framework Directive, publishing their findings in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 55, Issues 1–6, Pages 162–171). 35. Schneider TJ et al. (2019) evaluated the failure of regulations to constrain dog space use in threatened species’ beach habitats. Their research was published in the Journal of Environmental Planning and Management (Volume 63, Issue 6, Pages 1022–1036). 36. Staggs R and Pay JL (2019) provided an overview of cnidarian toxicity, with their findings accessible online. 37. Suthanthangjai M et al. (2013) compared survey approaches to track New Zealanders’ environmental perceptions, publishing their findings in the International Journal of Science and Society (Volume 13, Issue 4, Pages 25–40). 38. Tudor DT and Williams AT (2006) explored the rationale behind public beach selection along the coast of Wales, UK, publishing their findings in Area (Volume 38, Pages 153–164). 39. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) (2009) addressed marine litter as a global challenge in a report published in Nairobi, Kenya. 40. Ward NT et al. (2012) reviewed evidence-based treatment options for jellyfish stings in North America and Hawaii, publishing their findings in Annals of Emergency Medicine (Volume 60, Pages 399–414). 41. White M et al. (2016) discussed the health and well-being benefits of blue spaces, publishing their findings in the Journal of the Marine Biological Association of the United Kingdom (Volume 96, Issue 1, Pages 5–12). 42. Widmer WM and Reis RA (2010) conducted an experimental evaluation of beach ashtrays’ effectiveness in preventing marine contamination, publishing their findings in the Brazilian Archives of Biology and Technology (Volume 53, Pages 1205–1216). 43. Williams AT et al. (2016) analyzed the distribution of beach litter along the coastline of Cádiz, Spain, publishing their findings in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 107, Pages 77–87). 44. Winton DJ et al. (2020) focused on macroplastic pollution in freshwater environments, emphasizing public and policy action. Their study was published in Science of the Total Environment (Volume 704, Article 135242). 45. Wyles KJ et al. (2017) compared the impact of beach cleans to other coastal activities, publishing their findings in Environment and Behavior (Volume 49, Pages 509–535). 46. Zielinski S et al. (2019) critically reviewed beach cleaning methods and their impacts, publishing their findings in Marine Pollution Bulletin (Volume 139, Pages 390–410). 47. Zimmer J-Y et al. (2014) synthesized knowledge on the larval ecology of biting midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae), publishing their findings in Biotechnology, Agronomy, Society, and Environment (Volume 18, Issue 2, Pages 301–312). 48. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for recreational water quality aim to protect public health by ensuring the safe management of coastal and freshwater environments. These guidelines describe the potential adverse health impacts of recreational water use and provide recommendations for setting health-based targets, conducting risk assessments, and implementing monitoring systems. They also emphasize the health, well-being, and economic benefits of recreational water use while addressing environmental protection measures.
